newsitem.title: USA: Signs of U.S. economic pickup may be temporary.
newsitem.headline: Signs of U.S. economic pickup may be temporary.

text.p: Fears of inflation amid signs of stronger economic growth have rattled Wall Street but many experts say it is too soon to conclude the expansion is headed toward overheating.
One of the worries is that the Federal Reserve might become concerned enough to raise interest rates, although many central bank observers say such a move is not imminent.

"I think all the evidence of a pickup in growth is far too modest to cause concern," said economist Barry Bosworth of the Brookings Institution think tank. "No policy maker should act on this without a great deal more data."
Data showing robust job creation in December and continued low unemployment sent U.S. Treasury prices sharply lower Friday, temporarily taking stock prices down with them.
Jobs grew a hefty 262,000 last month as the jobless rate stood steady at 5.3 percent, the Labor Department reported.
That followed several other recent reports on housing, construction and manufacturing that have pointed to strength and unnerved inflation-wary bond traders.

"There is a question of how much underlying momentum the economy is generating," said Chris Varvares, president of the St. Louis forecasting firm Macroeconomic Advisers. "If this momentum we're seeing continues, there is almost no question you will see a rate hike."
Still, Varvares said there are reasons to believe any growth spurt might be temporary.
He and other economists believe the Fed will most certainly hold its fire until there is more evidence.

In a Reuter poll conducted Friday, 27 of 29 economists surveyed predicted no change in key interest rates at the next meeting of the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, on Feb. 4 and 5.
Indications that consumers, whose purchases make up roughly two-thirds of the economy, are not likely to go on a spending spree anytime soon is one limiting factor for growth.
"The consumer is probably not going to lead economic growth in 1997 but is along for the ride," Varvares said.
While surveys show consumers are upbeat about the economy, many of them are carrying high levels of debt, limiting their ability to ring up big purchases.

"In order to get this really rapid growth that some people are fearing, consumers are going to have to go into more debt," said economist James Annable of First Chicago-NBD Bank. "The data suggest they are already tapped out."
Reports from retailers of weaker-than-expected Christmas sales were evidence of the constraints on household spending.

So far, most Fed officials have downplayed concerns that the economy was set to overheat, predicting instead a moderate rate of growth of around 2 to 2-1/2 percent for 1997. Such a pace is what many at the Fed consider to be sustainable over time without fueling inflation.
So long as growth remains in that area, Fed Gov. Laurence Meyer suggested the central bank would have little inclination to alter its stance of steady rates.
"While there might be some danger in the forecast, that's enough to keep us alert but not enough to take us off the sidelines right now," he told reporters last weekend.
The economy grew by 2.1 percent in the third quarter of 1996. Government figures for fourth-quarter growth are due at the end of the month.

Looking at the inflation risks, Meyer and other officials have emphasized that the closely watched "core" Consumer Price Index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has been well-behaved, hovering near 30-year lows.

However, Fed Gov. Susan Phillips, whose comments in a speech Thursday were among the few to hint at any concern, cautioned that higher food and energy prices could also pose a risk to inflation should they persist.

On the commodity-price front, the latest figures from the Agriculture Department reinforced some fears of sustained food price rises. The data showed potential problems with the wheat supply, with winter wheat plantings at their lowest level since 1978.
